blocks.content: A multi-stage build lets a Dockerfile use several FROM stages, one to actually build your application (with all its heavy compilers and build tools), and a separate, much slimmer stage that only copies over the final compiled artifact. The full mechanics live in the Docker Build module, this topic covers the concept.

Compiling an application often requires tools you do not need at runtime: compilers, build caches, dev headers. A single-stage Dockerfile that installs all of that ends up shipping those build tools inside your production image too, bloating it for no runtime benefit.

blocks.alt: Build tools stay in the build stage, only the artifact moves forward

blocks.content: For compiled languages especially, the gap between a single-stage and a multi-stage image can be enormous, easily a gigabyte-plus image shrinking down to tens of megabytes, because the final stage never carries the compiler toolchain at all.

blocks.alt: The compiler toolchain never has to ship to production

blocks.content: Compiled languages like Go, Rust, and Java benefit the most from this pattern, since their build tooling is large and completely unnecessary once you have a finished binary or jar file. Interpreted languages like Python or Node.js benefit less dramatically, but can still use the same idea to separate dependency installation from the runtime image.

blocks.alt: Compiled languages see the biggest wins from this pattern

blocks.content: 4. What the Syntax Looks Like, at a Glance
blocks.text: 4. What the Syntax Looks Like, at a Glance

blocks.content: A multi-stage Dockerfile simply has more than one FROM line, each starting a new stage, with a later stage able to COPY --from= a named earlier stage to pull in just the files it actually needs.

blocks.alt: Multiple FROM lines, one final slim stage

blocks.content:
FROM golang:1.22 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o app .

FROM alpine
COPY --from=builder /src/app /app
CMD ["/app"]

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Multi-stage builds separate the heavy build environment from the slim final image, only the finished artifact crosses over between stages.
This pattern delivers the biggest wins for compiled languages, where the build toolchain is large and completely unneeded at runtime.
